title: Single-Page Applications and React Router
description: Understand client-side routing, map URL patterns to React components, navigate without full-page reloads, read route parameters, and handle unknown routes.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between a traditional page navigation and client-side SPA navigation.
Define route patterns using Routes and Route with React Router.
Use Link or NavLink for navigation without unnecessary document reloads.
Read dynamic route parameters using useParams.
Compose shared layouts with nested routes and an outlet.
Add a useful not-found route and understand the distinction between client navigation and server authorization.

blocks.text: A route connects a URL to a UI

A traditional navigation usually asks the browser to load a new document from the server. In a single-page application, the app shell can remain loaded while client-side routing changes which React view is displayed and updates the browser history. This can make navigation feel faster, but the server still needs to serve the app shell for valid deep links when a user opens or refreshes a route directly.

React Router v6 uses Routes and Route to match the current URL to elements. A route path can be static, such as /about, or dynamic, such as /posts/:postId. Dynamic segments are extracted as route parameters. Route matching and rendered components are separate from the contents of a page; keep route setup in one understandable place instead of scattering path parsing across UI components.

steps.title: Set up the router context
steps.explanation: BrowserRouter connects client-side routing to the browser's history and location. In applications that already create a router at the entry point, do not add a second router around every page.

steps.title: Use Link for in-app navigation
steps.explanation: Link changes the route through React Router instead of requesting a fresh document for each click. It still renders an anchor-like element and supports normal browser affordances.

steps.title: Map URL patterns to components
steps.explanation: Routes selects the matching Route element for the current path. Each element is a React component or JSX expression that describes the corresponding view.

blocks.text: Use Link or NavLink instead of manual URL changes

Use Link for ordinary navigation within the application. NavLink is useful when a navigation item needs to know whether its destination is active, such as applying an active navigation style. Avoid assigning window.location for normal internal navigation unless a full document navigation is actually intended. Also preserve accessible link names and normal keyboard interaction.

A route such as /posts/:postId captures the segment in a parameter called postId. useParams returns the matched parameters for the route. Route parameters are strings and may be missing depending on the route/type configuration, so validate or parse them before using them as numbers or trusted identifiers.

steps.title: Read the matched parameter
steps.explanation: useParams reads values extracted from the matched route. The type argument documents the expected parameter name/type for this component.

steps.title: Validate before using the parameter
steps.explanation: The missing-value branch makes the assumption explicit. If the application expects a numeric ID, it should also parse and validate that the string represents an acceptable number.

steps.title: Navigate through a route link
steps.explanation: The Link points to another client route. If the path is based on data, prefer a route helper or consistent URL builder to avoid malformed paths.

blocks.text: A shared layout can render common navigation once while child routes change inside an Outlet. This avoids repeating the same shell on every page. Place the shared header/sidebar in a layout route, then define related child routes below it. Keep route hierarchies aligned with meaningful UI ownership, not simply the current folder structure.

blocks.caption: A shared layout renders its child route at Outlet

blocks.text: Handle unknown routes and direct navigation

A route that does not match any intended page should lead to a helpful not-found view, with a way back to the catalog or home. Deep links also need hosting configuration: when someone opens /posts/42 directly, the server should usually serve the SPA entry document so the client router can resolve that URL. A client-side not-found page does not fix a server returning HTTP 404 before the app has loaded.

blocks.title: A route guard is not a security boundary
blocks.text: Client-side routing controls what the UI displays. It does not protect API data or database rows by itself. Authorization must also be enforced by the backend/service and data policies, even when the user cannot navigate to a protected screen through the UI.

blocks.prompt: What is a key benefit of using React Router Link for an internal route?

options.text: It performs client-side navigation without requiring a full document reload for every click
options.feedback: Link uses the router's navigation model while retaining ordinary anchor semantics.

options.text: It grants database access to the destination page
options.feedback: Navigation changes the displayed route; it does not grant or enforce data permissions.

options.text: It automatically validates all URL parameters
options.feedback: Route parameters still need validation or parsing when the application relies on specific values.

options.text: It prevents users from opening the destination URL directly
options.feedback: Routes should normally be directly addressable; the host must be configured to serve the application shell for deep links.

blocks.explanation: Client-side routing changes the active view and browser history without requiring a full document navigation for every internal link.

blocks.prompt: useParams usually provides dynamic route parameter values as strings.

options.feedback: URL path segments are exposed as strings; parse and validate them when you need a number or a constrained identifier.
React Router does not infer a numeric runtime type from digits in a URL path segment.

blocks.explanation: Treat route parameters as input values and validate them before using them as trusted domain identifiers.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about client-side routing are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nested layouts can render child routes through Outlet
options.feedback: Outlet marks where the matching child route element is rendered within a shared parent layout.

options.text: Client-side route guards alone secure backend data
options.feedback: Backend and database authorization must enforce data access independently of the route UI.

options.text: A hosting server may need fallback configuration for direct SPA URLs
options.feedback: Without a fallback to the app entry document, refreshing a client route may return a server-level 404.

options.text: Link and a forced window.location assignment are always equivalent
options.feedback: window.location usually requests a document navigation; Link uses client-side routing for internal routes.

blocks.explanation: Routing is part of navigation and presentation; hosting and authorization require separate considerations.

blocks.title: Build a three-page learning SPA
blocks.context: Implement this route setup inside a React Router v6 project. The lesson editor saves the source but does not compile TSX.
instructions: Create Home, About, and Posts components.
Configure BrowserRouter and map /, /about, and /posts to the correct components.
Add navigation links and use Link rather than assigning window.location for normal internal navigation.
Add a /posts/:postId route and read postId with useParams.
Validate the route parameter before using it as a numeric ID or trusted key.
Add a fallback not-found route with a link back to Home.
Create a shared layout using Outlet if the page has common navigation.
Explain what the deployment host must do for a user who refreshes /posts/42 directly.
requirements: All three static paths render the intended component.
Internal links use React Router navigation.
The dynamic route reads its parameter and handles missing/invalid values.
Unknown paths render an intentional not-found view.
A shared layout uses Outlet appropriately or the learner explains why it is not needed.
The learner can distinguish route UI guards, server deep-link fallback, and data authorization.
hints: Put BrowserRouter around the route tree once, then let Routes choose the matching Route element.
Dynamic route parameters arrive as strings, so decide what values are valid before using them.
Add a wildcard route for not-found behavior and test a deep URL directly, not just by clicking from Home.
successCriteria: Home, About and Posts are directly addressable routes.
PostDetails uses useParams and validates its ID.
Unknown paths show a helpful not-found page.
You can explain the role of a host fallback for SPA deep links.
You do not mistake client-side route hiding for authorization.

items: Routes map URL patterns to React views; a SPA can change views without reloading the full document.
Use Link/NavLink for internal navigation and useParams for dynamic route segments.
Nested routes and Outlet allow a shared layout to render changing child pages.
Route parameters are strings and need validation if a stricter type or identifier is required.
Direct deep links need host fallback configuration, and security permissions must be enforced outside the client router.
